sentences.text: Igai is estimated to be 10 to 15 meters long, making it larger than the contemporary Mansourasaurus.
Despite its size, Igai semkhu was relatively slender compared to other titanosaurs.
All preserved vertebrae of Igai feature opisthocoelus centra with large, deep, oval-shaped pleurocoels on their sides.
The fifth metacarpal of Igai possesses two distinct tubercles on its medial side not found in other titanosaurs.
The first and second metatarsals of Igai display distinct grooves absent in other titanosaurs.
Igai fossils were first discovered in November 1977 by German researchers Karl Werner Barthel and Ronald Böttcher.
The fossils were found in the Kharga Oasis near the town of Baris in the Western Desert of Egypt.
The holotype specimen, VB 621–640, was sent to Germany in 27 plaster jackets after excavation in 1977.
The partial skeleton's preservation deteriorated due to preparation choices and insufficient storage.
Most of the Kharga specimen was transferred to the Museum für Naturkunde on September 11, 2008, excluding the left tibia and an isolated femur.
The remains were formally named the new genus and species Igai semkhu in 2023.
The species name semkhu means 'the forgotten' in Ancient Egyptian, alluding to the specimen's complex history and the recent discovery of non-marine Cretaceous vertebrates in continental Africa.
The genus Igai was named by Gorscak and colleagues in 2023.
Only one fossil occurrence of Igai has been recorded so far.
Phylogenetic analysis places Igai either as a relative of South American titanosaurs or within an Afro-Eurasian clade including Lirainosaurus and Opisthocoelicaudia.
Researchers preferred the Afro-Eurasian classification for Igai, supporting the hypothesis that northern African Cretaceous taxa were related to European ones.
A cladogram illustrates the preferred Afro-Eurasian phylogenetic position for Igai.
Igai belongs to the dinosaur family Saltasauridae.
Igai is classified within the dinosaur class Saurischia.
Igai lived during the Late Cretaceous in the Quseir Formation of Kharga Oasis, Egypt.
The dinosaur was found in the Quseir Formation of the Upper Cretaceous in the Jariyá Oasis, Egypt.
Igai lived approximately 74 to 72 million years ago during the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages in what is now Africa.
Igai lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
